title: Electrochemistry
standard_text: Oxidation and reduction; oxidation numbers; balancing redox half-reactions; galvanic cells and standard reduction potentials; electrolytic cells and electrolysis; batteries, fuel cells and corrosion. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Chemistry, Grade 12, University Preparation (SCH4U), Strand F: Electrochemistry)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Chemistry (SCH4U) worksheets on electrochemistry: oxidation numbers, redox half-reactions, galvanic cells, standard reduction potentials, electrolysis, batteries and corrosion. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain.
body_html:
How to think about it

Oxidation is the loss of electrons (oxidation number goes up); reduction is the gain of electrons (oxidation number goes down). To balance a redox reaction, write the two half-reactions, balance atoms and charge with electrons, and make the electrons equal.

In a galvanic cell, a spontaneous reaction makes electricity: oxidation at the anode (−), reduction at the cathode (+), and electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; a positive value means spontaneous. An electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.

Example

Oxidation number of Mn in MnO₄⁻?

4 × (−2) = −8

Mn − 8 = −1

Answer: +7

Example

Zn²⁺/Zn E° = −0.76 V; Cu²⁺/Cu E° = +0.34 V. E°cell?

Cu is reduced (cathode).

0.34 − (−0.76)

Answer: +1.10 V

Common mistakes

  • Saying the anode is always positive: in a galvanic cell it is negative.
  • Multiplying E° values when you multiply a half-reaction.
  • Mixing up the oxidizing agent (it is reduced) and the reducing agent (it is oxidized).

faq.q: Why does iron rust faster near salt water?
faq.a: Salt water is a good electrolyte, so the redox reactions of corrosion happen faster.

faq.q: What does a salt bridge do?
faq.a: It lets ions move between the half-cells so the charges stay balanced and the current keeps flowing.

items.q: Is this change oxidation or reduction: NO₃⁻ → NO₂ (in acid)?

items.q: Use E° values (Mg²⁺/Mg: −2.37 V; Pb²⁺/Pb: −0.130 V). Is it feasible for the oxidized form in Mg²⁺/Mg to oxidize the reduced form in Pb²⁺/Pb under standard conditions?
items.e: A reaction is feasible when the oxidizing agent's E° is more positive than the reducing agent's (E°<sub>cell</sub> > 0).

items.q: A cell is made from the Mg²⁺/Mg (E° = −2.37 V) and MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ (E° = 1.51 V) half-cells. Which half-cell is the negative electrode?
items.e: The more negative E° is the negative electrode, where oxidation happens.

items.q: Calculate the standard e.m.f. of a cell made from the Mg²⁺/Mg (E° = −2.37 V) and Ni²⁺/Ni (E° = −0.250 V) half-cells.

items.q: How much charge passes when a current of 3 A flows for 21 minutes?
Which product forms at the positive electrode (anode) during electrolysis of molten lead bromide?
items.e: Halide ions give the halogen; otherwise oxygen forms.

items.q: How much charge passes when a current of 7 A flows for 41 minutes?
Dilute aqueous sodium chloride is electrolyzed with inert carbon electrodes. What happens at the anode (positive electrode)?
items.e: Negative ions go to the anode. In dilute solutions OH⁻ is discharged (oxygen); concentrated chloride gives chlorine; a copper anode dissolves.

items.q: Which product forms at the positive electrode (anode) during electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (brine)?
items.e: Halide ions give the halogen; otherwise oxygen forms.

items.q: Which product forms at the negative electrode (cathode) during electrolysis of molten aluminum oxide?
items.e: Molten: the metal forms. Aqueous: hydrogen forms unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen.

items.q: Using λ°(cation) = 106 and λ°(anion part) = 153 S cm² mol⁻¹, what is Λ°<sub>m</sub> of MgCl₂? (Kohlrausch's law)
items.e: Λ°m = λ°+ + λ°− = 259 S cm² mol⁻¹.

items.q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolyzed with inert carbon electrodes. What is formed at the cathode (negative electrode)?
items.e: Positive ions go to the cathode. In aqueous solutions of reactive metals, hydrogen is discharged instead of the metal.

items.q: In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which is the reducing agent?
items.e: CO loses electrons (is oxidized), so it is the reducing agent.

items.q: What is the oxidation state of C in CH<sub>3</sub>OH?
items.e: Oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides), hydrogen +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the total equals the charge on the species.

items.q: Which pair of metals gives the largest voltage in a simple cell?
items.e: The further apart the metals are in the reactivity series, the larger the voltage.

items.q: A simple cell is made from zinc and silver dipped in an electrolyte. Which metal is the negative terminal?
items.e: The more reactive metal loses electrons more easily, so it is the negative terminal.

items.q: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which is the oxidizing agent?
items.e: Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidizing agent; Zn is the reducing agent.

items.q: In a simple cell made of aluminum and copper, in which direction do electrons flow in the external wire?
items.e: Electrons flow from the more reactive metal (negative) to the less reactive metal.

items.q: Which electrolyte's Λ°<sub>m</sub> cannot be found by extrapolating to zero concentration?
c: a strong electrolyte such as KCl
a weak electrolyte such as ethanoic acid
items.e: Kohlrausch's law is used instead.

items.q: Why can KMnO₄ act only as an oxidizing agent?
c: Mn is in its highest oxidation state, +7
Mn is at its lowest state
items.e: It can only be reduced.

items.q: In Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂, which is the oxidizing agent?
items.e: Cl₂ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidizing agent; KI (I⁻) is the reducing agent.

items.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which is the reducing agent?
items.e: H₂ loses electrons (is oxidized), so it is the reducing agent.

items.q: In a simple cell made of magnesium and iron, in which direction do electrons flow in the external wire?
items.e: Electrons flow from the more reactive metal (negative) to the less reactive metal.
